events.text: You have worn faces for a season at a time: someone's cousin, a peddler's widow, a monk who owed money. They do for a market. Today you lay in the reeds and watched an old pair on the dyke argue over one bag of salt, the same argument, you could tell, for thirty years. Neither of them was lying. You have a bead in your mouth that has cost other people a good deal. You would like very much to be argued with.

choices.text: Turn over at the crossroads, and begin a face that can last

effects.log: A face for a season is easy. For a lifetime it needs bones, a bad tooth, and somewhere to go on the days when nobody is looking. You start on it as you would a burrow, by digging.

choices.text: Stay in your fur. Salt is not for you

effects.log: You lie in the reeds until they have gone. They are still at it when they pass the mound, faintly. There are easier ways to be warm, and you know every one of them by name.

events.text: You take the chin from a ferryman and the brow from a woman selling combs. You go down to the market in it, and a stranger stops you and says you are the image of her cousin. Another says the same, of his. It is a good sign. Then a brown dog by the butcher's gets up, looks at you, and leaves the market. It does not bark. It just goes, as one goes from a room when someone has said something unfortunate.

choices.text: Go back, and stand downwind of the dog until it tires of leaving

effects.log: It takes nine market days. It never does stop leaving. But the butcher has stopped looking to see why, and you have learned which side of the lane the dogs are not on.

choices.text: Go home. You have got what you came for

effects.log: You go home and take off the chin. The market goes on telling itself about your cousin. Nobody has ever said that you looked like somebody, and you lie on the mound quite pleased.

events.text: On the hill road an old salt peddler with a forked stick is resting his load. He does not look up. "Evening, old one," he says. "Your left ear is high." You say that you do not know what he means, in a very good voice. He puts a pinch of salt on the stone between you, and waits. "Long walk to a house," he says, "on those." He looks at your feet. Then he sells you a bag, at the proper price.

choices.text: Fix the ear. He has told you something for nothing

effects.log: It takes a night, and the ear is better. You do not know why he did that. You keep the bag. Salt is bad for you, and you take a little every day now, to have the habit.

choices.text: Follow him some way, and see where he sleeps

effects.log: He sleeps on his back in the open with his stick across his chest, snoring, and a yellow dog on his feet. You go away again. Nobody has ever been so little afraid of you, and it spoils your whole week.

events.text: It has taken you a very long time to learn this, and it is in no book. Nobody looks at a plain face. You have been going about like a court painting, with every traveller walking into a ditch, and it has kept you on the run. So you take a tooth and crook it. You give the nose an opinion. You go down to the well looking like somebody's reasonable relation, and you draw a bucket. No one looks up.

choices.text: Draw another, and carry it to somebody's door

effects.log: You carry it for an old man with a bad back, and he says thank you without looking round. You stand in his yard with your hands empty. You have never got away with anything so thoroughly.

choices.text: Keep the good face underneath, just in case

effects.log: You keep it folded behind the plain one, like a coin in a shoe. It makes the jaw ache. It is a long time before you stop feeling for it with your tongue.

events.text: {npc} carves the masks for the village's spring dance. {He} sits at the crossroads with a block of alder and {his} knife, and everyone who goes past gets looked at, and you go past. {He} stops cutting. {He} looks at your face longer than anyone ever has, and you feel it tighten, down to the bad tooth. "Would you sit for me?" {he} says. "I have been trying to get that for eleven years. I don't know what it is."

choices.text: Sit. A face that cannot stand being looked at will not last

effects.log: You sit on an upturned basket in the sun for three hours, with the Bead cold in your mouth. {He} does not talk. It is the most dangerous afternoon of your life, and you come back the next day.

choices.text: Say that you have a long way to go, and go

effects.log: You are over the hill by dark, with your ear aching. There will be other crossroads. That one has a block of alder on it with a chin half done, and it is a very good chin.

events.text: The mask is done. {npc} turns it round on {his} knee in the last of the sun, and you are looking at the most accurate thing you have ever seen. Every line in it is yours, and it looks like nobody. {He} curses, quietly and at length. "It is like carving water. Everyone who sees it says it is their cousin." {He} throws it on the pile, reaches for a new block, and looks up. "Same time tomorrow?"

choices.text: Come tomorrow. And the day after

effects.log: You have sat for seven masks by the time the rains come. {He} has started to bring you something to eat, and to talk while {he} works, about wood, mostly. You go home each night and check the whole face over.

choices.text: Take that one off the pile when {he} is not looking

effects.log: It is under your arm when you go. You set it on the mound, and you look at it by moonlight for a long while. It looks back. It has no idea either.

events.text: {npc}'s old aunt has asked you to dinner, to look at you. You have eaten rice before, as one eats a hot stone to prove a point. The bead sits under your tongue, and you have to eat round it. The aunt is watching your hands. There are three hens in the yard outside the door. You are not looking at them. You are not looking at them so hard that your ears ache. "You have a good appetite," says the aunt.

choices.text: Have a second bowl, and say something about the weather

effects.log: It goes down like wet sand. You say that it looks like rain. The aunt allows that it does. That is the most human thing you have ever said, and you are sick in the reeds all the way home.

choices.text: Go back for one hen, in the night. Only one

effects.log: It is very good. In the morning there are feathers, and a long talk in the yard about foxes. {npc} mentions it with a smile while {he} cuts. You smile also. There is a small feather in your teeth, and you find it later.

events.text: A wedding, before the whole village, in a face. They have shut up the dogs for the noise. {npc} carved the wooden goose, and it looks rather surprised. You stand across the mat. You have to drink water from one half of a gourd, and {he} from the other, with the bead in your mouth. At the back of the crowd an old salt peddler has brought a bag of salt, puts it on the table, looks at your left ear, and lifts a cup.

choices.text: Bow. Drink the water. Swallow nothing but the water

effects.log: It goes round the bead and down. {He} looks at you over the rim of the gourd, very pleased with the day. The whole village says you look just like someone in their family. You are, as of this afternoon.

choices.text: At the third bow, remember something you left on the fire

effects.log: You walk out past the shut-up dogs, and they scream at you through the wall. They find the robe in the reeds. {He} keeps the goose. It has no one to look surprised at.

events.text: You sleep with your face to the wall. You have to. A breath goes out of a sleeper and the bead turns toward it in your mouth, by itself, like a plant toward a window; it has made a good many people pale in its time. So every night of your life here you lie on your side, away, with your teeth shut. {npc} has never said anything. Tonight {he} puts a hand flat on your back, leaves it there, and goes to sleep.

choices.text: Lie still, and stay turned away

effects.log: You lie like that till morning, with your shoulder gone dead. {He} thinks you are a cold person, on the whole, and has decided to put up with it. You have never been given anything so large.

choices.text: Turn over, for a moment, and just see

effects.log: It is one breath, and it goes in before you can close your mouth. It tastes like new bread. {He} wakes up tired, and says {he} must be getting old. You stand in the yard in the cold until your hands stop.

events.text: {npc} has brought home a puppy, a yellow thing with enormous feet, inside {his} jacket, and {he} is as happy as you have ever seen {him}. "We have always needed a dog," {he} says. You have spent years arranging that you should not. You have told a story about a bite when you were small. The puppy puts its head out. It sees you. It has not learned yet that it should be afraid. It has not far to go.

choices.text: Hold out your hand. Let it get used to you, if it can

effects.log: It shakes for a month. It sleeps across the door, growls in its sleep, and will not eat from your hand. But it stays. {He} says it is only nervous. You have never worked so hard on anything as on that dog.

choices.text: Say that it is the puppy or you, and mean it

effects.log: You have never asked {him} for anything, so {he} takes it back. {He} does not speak for two days, and then {he} does, about wood. There is a small hollow by the gate that {he} dug for its water. You walk round it.

events.text: You have to age. Nobody warned you about this. You put in the first grey at thirty, one hair at a time, and the lines by the mouth in the order you saw them on the neighbours. You forgot a whole year once, and someone remarked on your skin. Last autumn you gave yourself a bad knee, on the left, and it is the best work you have ever done. It aches before rain. You have started to limp in the reeds, with no one there.

choices.text: Let {npc} rub it, with the liniment

effects.log: There is nothing wrong with that knee. There never was. {He} has strong thumbs, and {he} does it carefully every wet night, year on year, and it does help. You cannot explain that to anyone.

choices.text: Say that it is nothing, and go and do the next hair

effects.log: You do the next hair, by lamplight, in a bronze mirror, with your tongue between your teeth. Nobody has ever been so careful about going grey.

events.text: {npc} is working late by the lamp, on a mask. You bring in the tea. You have crossed this room ten thousand times, and you know where a lamp puts you. But you are tired, the knee hurts, and you take the short way, by the paper door. Your shadow goes up the paper, far too wide behind. You stop. {He} has stopped cutting. {He} does not turn {his} head at once. You have about the length of one breath.

choices.text: Set down the tray. Stay where you are, and let the lamp burn

effects.log: {He} turns. {He} looks at the wall for a long while, and {he} counts. {He} is a carver, and {he} counts them twice. "The second from the left wants work," {he} says, not at all steadily. {He} picks up the knife again, and {he} does not put you out.

choices.text: Blow it out. Say that you have been meaning to save on oil

effects.log: It is very dark, and {he} says nothing, and you hand {him} the tea. You both drink it. {He} feels {his} way to bed. The next day {he} moves the lamp to the other wall.

choices.text: Go. Through the door, in your fur, before it is light

effects.log: You leave the tray on the floor, with the tea still warm. Somebody's dog howls after you as far as the second dyke. It is quite possibly the first thing one has ever said to you in friendship.

events.text: Fifteen years, and {npc} has got it. {He} brings it to you in both hands, shaking: your face, the one you made, in alder and lacquer, exactly right. It does not look like anyone's cousin now. "There," {he} says. "That is who I married. Look at that." This morning your left ear was high again, and you had to push it back. The mask fits your hand. It is better work than you are, and it will never slip.

choices.text: Take off your own, and show {him} what is under it

effects.log: {He} looks from one to the other, for a long, terrible time. Then {he} reaches out, not to the fur but to the jaw, and feels along it with {his} thumb. "I could do that better," {he} says, and starts to cry. You have no idea what has just happened.

choices.text: Say that it is beautiful. Hang it on the wall

effects.log: It hangs across from the bed for the rest of your life, with the lamplight on it. {He} looks at it sometimes when you come in, and then at you, comparing. The face slips a little more each year, and {he} has begun to frown.

choices.text: Set it on the pillow, and go. {He} has what {he} wanted

effects.log: You leave before light. It is quite true: {he} has what {he} wanted. You tell yourself so at the crossroads, on your way up to the mounds. It would be easier if you had not kept the bad knee.

events.text: There is a child, named {bk_child}, and you have counted everything. No ears, no tail, nothing at the end of the spine but a child. {npc} is asleep with {his} mouth open. You hold it in the dark and look, and it comes to you what is strange. It has no face yet. Nobody made this. Nobody chose the nose. Tomorrow the whole lane will come, and each will say it looks like them, and for once they will know as much as you.

choices.text: Keep your mouth shut, and your breath away from it, always

effects.log: You hold it at the length of your arm, and feed it with your head turned. It will never know why you smell of salt. You are the most careful person anyone in this lane has ever seen with a baby, and they all say so.

choices.text: Breathe on it, once. Only to see what it does

effects.log: It sneezes, looks offended, and goes back to sleep. A small bright taste comes back to you from it, and you swallow that. You will be doing the sums on it for a very long time.

events.text: A second, named {bk_child}, after a long hard night, and your face held. Just. There is an old rule that every vixen tells the cubs: two births a face will bear. At a third it slips, in front of the midwife, all at once. You have been told this by better foxes than you. You lie there getting your jaw back where it goes. {npc} is at the door with a bowl and a huge smile. "Two," {he} says. "Let us have a full house."

choices.text: Say that two is plenty

effects.log: You say it, and you go on saying it. You turn to the wall a little further. {He} thinks it is the pain, and {he} is very gentle, and {he} will never know how close you came to telling {him} the count.

choices.text: Smile back. You will cross that dyke when you come to it

effects.log: It is a very good smile, with the crooked tooth. You lie awake afterwards working out how much Bead it would take to hold a face through a third. The answer is somebody else's breath.

events.text: {bk_child} is seven, and you have checked all this time. Nothing. {bk_child} has {bk_love}'s ears, and the same face every single morning, lies badly, and goes red. Any dog in the lane will come and lie across those small feet with a sigh, and look at you over them. You hold your own jaw in place at breakfast, across the table, and watch how easy it is. You would not have thought that you could envy this.

choices.text: Be glad of it. Teach {bk_child} nothing

effects.log: You teach nothing. {bk_child} grows up with a red face and loud opinions, and dogs, and is never once mistaken for anybody else. You could watch that all day. You do.

choices.text: Try, one time, to see if it can be taught

effects.log: You show {bk_child} how to do a neighbour's walk. It is very bad, the neighbour is not fooled, and the whole lane laughs. {bk_child} laughs too. You put that away, relieved by how much it hurts.

events.text: The old mother of the house has died, and for nine days {bk_love} has not eaten. This morning {bk_child}, seven years old, goes into the back room and comes out walking slowly, one hand at the small of the back. It is her face, small and exact: the mouth, the eyelid. She takes up the bowl in both hands and says, "Eat something, you fool," in that voice. And {bk_love} does. The dog gets up, and leaves the room.

choices.text: Take the child up to the mounds tonight, and tell it what that costs

effects.log: You sit in your own fur on the cold grass, and a small face looks at you and is not surprised. You tell it about the bead, the debt and the wall. It asks if it did wrong. You have been alive all these years, and you do not know.

choices.text: Wipe its face with your sleeve until it is its own again, and say nothing

effects.log: You rub until the child complains. {bk_love} is still eating, and crying into it. Nobody will speak of this. But the child looks at you across the room, out of its own eyes, and you both know who the other one is.

events.text: {npc} has gone nearly blind, which is hard on a carver. {He} still has the thumbs. {He} sits on the step with {his} face up to the sun, calls you over, and takes your jaw in {his} hands, as {he} has been meaning to. {He} goes over it slowly, up to the left ear, and stops. "You have been getting this wrong since spring," {he} says. "It was better at forty. You should have asked me."

choices.text: Ask {him} what to do about the ear

effects.log: {He} shows you, with {his} thumb, pressing. It is nearly right. "There," {he} says. "I have wanted to do that for thirty years." You do not ask how long. {He} does not tell you. You sit in the sun with your whole head ringing.

choices.text: Take {his} hand, and put it on the fur, while there is time

effects.log: {He} feels it a long while, down to where it stops, and {he} laughs, an old dry laugh. "Well, I could not have got that in alder," {he} says. You stay in your own skin on that step, for as long as {he} wants to go on holding it.

events.text: They bury {bk_love} on the south slope. The lane comes, and each one tells you that you must eat. You stand there in the old face with the bad knee. You have held it longer than most foxes live, and nobody is left who can tell if the ear is high. At the back, a yellow dog sits down, a little way off, and looks at you, and for the first time does not get up to go. There is no one here that you have got to fool.

choices.text: Keep the face. Give it a thousand days more

effects.log: You do them one at a time. You sit by that mound each evening, in the face, and eat rice. You go grey on schedule. Nobody in the lane knows why you are still so careful, and there is no one left to ask.

choices.text: Take it off, there at the graveside, when they have gone

effects.log: It comes away in one piece. You fold it up, push it into the new earth with your own nose, and go up the hill on four feet. The knee still aches, on the left. It always will.

events.text: Eighty years on, you walk down through the county in a face. They are everywhere. {bk_child}'s people do very well: go-betweens, clerks of the better sort, the one you send for when two houses are not speaking. Everybody likes them, and no one could tell you what they look like. They have never had any luck with dogs. One of them has just sold you some rice, and reminded you of your cousin.

choices.text: Buy some more, and look closely at the left ear

effects.log: It is very slightly high. Nobody else would see. You pay the proper price, you say it looks like rain, and you go up the road with your whole face grinning, and you have to stop and put it right.

choices.text: Keep walking. They are doing well without you

effects.log: You go past without slowing. The one at the rice stall looks up after you have gone, looks all round the market, and goes back to weighing. Behind you, somebody's dog has got up.

events.text: One of {bk_child}'s people, a magistrate's go-between, comes along the hill road at dusk. There is a salt peddler on the stone, the old one's grandchild, and you are watching from the mound. The peddler studies the go-between's left ear. Then the peddler looks straight at the hill, at you, lifts a cup of water, and sells the go-between a bag of salt at the proper price.

choices.text: Come down, and stand beside the road in your fur

effects.log: The go-between goes by, and does not see. The peddler does. You nod to one another, two old firms that have done business for a long time. You have never been so respectably hated.

choices.text: Go round by the mounds, and be somewhere else by morning

effects.log: It is the oldest rule you know. In the morning there is a pinch of salt on the stone where you had been sitting, and you do not know how that was done.

events.text: You gave up keeping house sixty years ago. You are on the hill road in a good plain face, and a young salt peddler, {npc}, comes up with a load, and stops. {He} puts down {his} stick. "Your tail is out," {he} says. "Three or four of them. You want to see to that." Then {he} sits down, gets out {his} rice, and holds out half. Nobody has ever been so rude to you, and you are so tired.

choices.text: Let the face go, sit down in your fur, and eat it

effects.log: It is terrible rice, and you tell {him} so in your own voice, which you have not used in ages. {He} nods. {He} comes that way every month after that, and there is not one thing you have to keep up. You have no idea how to do it.

choices.text: Thank {him}, tidy your tail, and go on up the road

effects.log: You are polite about it, and you keep the face. {He} watches you out of sight, chewing. You do not take that road again, and you miss it on the days you are being very convincing.

events.text: Someone is sitting at the foot of your mound at the full moon, easing one leg. They are a stranger to you. They look like everyone. They have a bad knee, on the left, and they say that it aches before rain, and that they get it from their people. You stare. A knee like that was made out of nothing, one wet autumn, by a fox with a house. They rub it with their thumbs, and look up at you, as at a distant relation.

choices.text: Sit down beside them in your fur, and ask about the weather

effects.log: "It looks like rain," they say. You allow that it does. There is no dog for three valleys, and they stay till the moon is down. Neither of you asks a name. They have very good manners, and you know where they got them.

choices.text: Tell them there is nothing wrong with it

effects.log: They look at you, and they flex it. "I know that," they say. "It still aches." They get up, not quite straight, and take the road with a limp that took years to get right, and it is perfect.

events.text: The neighbours all say that you take after them, over the wall, each of them quite sure. You are six, and you have just noticed about dogs. There is a dog in every yard in this lane, and when you go in it gets up, not fast, and goes out the other way. You thought all dogs did that. {npc}, who has been about this house for ever, watches you trying to give one a rice cake, at the length of your arm.

choices.text: Ask {him} why it will not come

effects.log: "It has got a good nose," {npc} says, "and not much else. Do not mind it." {He} takes the rice cake and eats it, looking at you the whole time, from one side and then the other.

choices.text: Eat the cake, and say that you never liked dogs

effects.log: You say it very well, with your nose up. {npc} is quite convinced, or looks it. It is the first time you have noticed how easy it is to be convincing.

events.text: You have been walking home with the cooper's boy. You come in for dinner, and {npc} looks up and puts down {his} spoon. "Whose mouth is that?" {he} says. {He} takes you to the water butt, and you look in. It is yours, more or less. But you are holding it to one side, as the cooper's boy does, and you were a different child at noon. You have been doing this for years. It is why they all like you so much.

choices.text: Try to put it back. Ask {him} what it was like before

effects.log: {He} looks at you for a good long time, and {he} cannot quite tell you. You stand at the butt till dark, trying out your mouth, and you are not sure which one was first. You pick the plainest.

choices.text: Wipe it off. Do the next one better

effects.log: You can do the whole schoolroom by spring, one at a time, just enough that nobody sees. You are the most popular child anyone has ever heard of, and you have no idea what you like to eat.

events.text: An old woman stops you at the well and calls you by a name. It is not your name. It is the name of a son who died at the river a year ago. You are standing as that son stood, it seems, with those shoulders, and a hand on your cheek. The old woman is so glad. You can feel it going into you like warm soup. All you have got to do is say yes. {npc}, across the well, has stopped with the rope in {his} hands.

choices.text: Say yes, just this once

effects.log: The old woman goes home walking like someone young. You feel wonderful for three days, and you have a feeling of having eaten. {npc} does not talk to you until the moon has changed.

choices.text: Say that the old woman has the wrong child. Step back, and change your shoulders

effects.log: The hand drops. You see it happen, all at once: a stranger's child is what is seen. "Forgive me," says the old woman. {npc} puts {his} hand on your head. You feel hungry for no reason.

events.text: You wake in your sixteenth year with something in your mouth, under your tongue. It is small and smooth, like a grain of rice sucked for a long while. You take it out, and by noon it has come back. Your shadow is not quite right, if a lamp is on it. {npc} looks in your mouth, as one does with a horse, and closes it for you. "Come up to the mounds tonight," {he} says. "It is time you heard who kept this house."

choices.text: Go up and hear it

effects.log: A face, worn for thirty years. {bk_line}, born into it and none the wiser. And {bk_anc}, who used to lie with its face to the wall. You sit on the cold grass. It explains the dogs, at least.

choices.text: Spit it in the well, and stay in bed

effects.log: You spit it in the well every morning for a year. The well is very sweet that year. You stay away from lamps, on the whole. {npc} lets you alone, and it is quite a normal way to be.

events.text: Everybody likes you. You have been to eleven weddings this year as somebody's friend from school. When two households are not speaking they send you, and each of them comes away thinking you took their side. Today the district clerk has had a robbery, and asks the lane to describe the stranger seen talking to the servant. It was you, being pleasant. They describe eleven different people. {npc} is quiet.

choices.text: Go and tell the clerk that it was you, and what you saw

effects.log: It takes a while to convince the clerk. The clerk asks you twice to come back, and cannot quite recall your name. They catch the thief. You have made a friend in the county, and that is not a safe thing.

choices.text: Say nothing. Be at the twelfth wedding

effects.log: It is a lovely wedding. Someone's old aunt says that you have the eyes of a certain brother. You dance. You have a different set by the end of the week, and you are getting quicker.

events.text: Two of your best friends have met at last. You can hear them through the wall. "Loves eel. Cannot stand a crowd. A very quiet person." "Who? Hates eel. Never happier than at a festival." They are not angry, only puzzled. They come out and look at you. You have a plate of eel in your hand. {npc} crosses the yard, takes it from you, eats it, and waits to see what you will do.

choices.text: Tell them you have no idea if you like eel

effects.log: It is the first true thing either of them has ever heard from you. One of them laughs, and one does not come back. The one who laughed makes you try everything on the table, and writes it down.

choices.text: Laugh, and say something that suits them both

effects.log: It takes you about four breaths. By the time the rice comes, they are both sure they were mistaken about the eel. {npc} chews, looks at you, and swallows. You have never felt so alone at so good a party.

events.text: The lane has had three pale people this winter. It is not you. It is some fox on the ridge with no manners. But there is going to be a hunt, and the whole village has come to your door, because you are the one who gets things organised. They would like a list, and the torches, and the dogs. "What would we do without you?" says the headman. The dogs have already left. {npc} shuts {his} eyes.

choices.text: Organise it. Send them over the wrong ridge, and go up at night to warn it off

effects.log: It is the best hunt the district has had. Nobody catches anything. You find the other one on the ridge at night, young and afraid of you, and you tell it what it is doing to that village. It goes. Everybody thanks you.

choices.text: Organise it properly. You have a house to keep

effects.log: You do it properly, with the right dogs and the right ridge. They bring it down in two days, a small young thing, and they show it to you, because you arranged it all. You say well done. You go home, and you cannot get your face to sit right.

events.text: {npc} has been watching you across the room. You know exactly what {he} wants, and you are already getting up to fetch it. You always do. No one has ever been so well understood, and {he} has said so. "Sit down," {he} says. "I have been married to you all these years, and I could not pick you out of a crowd. What do you look like when nobody is there?" {He} moves the lamp nearer. You know where a lamp puts you.

choices.text: Stand where the lamp wants you, and tell {him} the rest

effects.log: {He} looks at the wall for a long time. "Well, that is something," {he} says, in a flat voice. "Now. What do you want for dinner?" You do not know. You sit down and try to think, and {he} waits. It is the kindest thing anyone has ever done to you.

choices.text: Say something that makes {him} laugh. Move the lamp back

effects.log: It is a very good joke, and it was the right one. {He} laughs until {he} forgets. {He} will ask again in about four years, you know what you will say, and you lie down with your face to the wall.

events.text: {npc} has come in to dinner doing the neighbour's walk. {He} has got the hip. {He} looks up at you to see if it is funny, with {his} mouth a little to one side, in a way that it was not this morning. Out in the yard the dog that has been with this house for nine years stands up, looks in at the door, and goes to lie on the far side of the woodpile. You have a spoon in your hand. It is a very small thing to stop.

choices.text: Sit {him} down. Tell {him} what it is, and whose mouth to keep

effects.log: You tell {him} about mouths, and dogs, and the wall. {He} listens very attentively, with your own expression. You take {his} chin and turn it back, {he} lets you, and it stays for nearly a week.

choices.text: Laugh. It is funny

effects.log: {He} is delighted, and {he} does you next. It is very good. It is better than you are. The dog does not come back for some days. You go on laughing for quite a while after {he} has stopped.

events.text: {npc} walks into the inn with a yellow dog at {his} heel, old and lame. There is a room in every district, {he} will tell you, that a dog leaves. {He} has spent nine years walking into rooms. Just now the dog has looked at you, got up, and limped out. {npc} watches it go. Then {he} looks round the table, quite slowly, and sits down opposite you with a friendly face, and asks what you are drinking.

choices.text: Take it outside, and have it out with {him}

ok.log: You are not where {he} is hitting, and then you are behind {him}. {He} sits in the yard, breathing hard, and looks delighted. "Nine years," {he} says. "You have no idea." {He} will be back. But {he} goes now, and the dog limps after.

fail.log: There is a net in the coat. You had not seen that, with all you see. You get away through the reeds with a cut along your ribs. The dog sits down to watch you go. "Thanks," says {npc}. "That is the first one."

choices.text: Buy {him} a drink. Be the best company {he} has ever had

effects.log: It is no trouble. You know what {he} wants to talk about within a minute, and by midnight you have made {him} laugh until {he} coughed. {He} clasps your arm at the door, and takes your name. It is the wrong one.

events.text: {npc} again, twelve years on, at your gate with no dog. It died in the spring. {He} has a bad chest. "You know me better than anyone living," {he} says. "You have always been one town ahead of me, and kind about it. You know how I worked it out? Nobody is this easy to get on with." {He} sits on the step. "A court physician pays for the bead. I have asked nicely, because it is you. I do have the net in the coat."

choices.text: Finish it, at the back of the woodshed

ok.log: It takes no time at all. You know where {he} is going to be before {he} does. You bury {him} by the road, you say a few words, and they are exactly right, which is the worst of it.

fail.log: {He} has had twelve years to think about you. You go out through the wall with your chest stove in and your face left behind. {He} stands looking at where it slipped off you, quite tenderly, and does not follow.

choices.text: Sit down beside {him}, and take off the face

effects.log: It is the only thing you have got that {he} never saw. {He} looks at it for a long time, coughing. "You are very small," {he} says. "I thought you would be bigger." {He} does not touch the coat, and in the morning {he} goes away.

events.text: There is a student staying at the inn, pale already, and not from you. You pass that door at night, and you stop. It is the breath. It smells like new bread, all the way down the passage, and your whole mouth has come awake around the small hard thing in it. You have eaten today. This is not that. {npc} has come out with a lamp, stands between you and the door without seeming to, and asks how you are sleeping.

choices.text: Go up to the mounds instead, at the full moon, and breathe that

effects.log: It is thin and cold and it takes all night, and the bead brightens a very little. You are quite steady in the morning. The student goes home unharmed. You know how near it was, and so does {npc}.

choices.text: Be one person, all this year. One name, one voice

effects.log: It is harder than it should be. People find you a bit dull that year, and ask if you are unwell. You do not go down that passage. There is a hollow feeling under your tongue, and it goes, mostly.

events.text: This morning you look into the water, and it takes you some time to find the one you went to bed in. It has started slipping: an ear, a lid. It is a full moon tonight, and it has got very clear to you that something on the hill knows your real name, which you do not. {npc} has taken to knocking before {he} comes in. You could go up and see. You could stop looking in water.

choices.text: Go up at moonrise, with nothing on your face at all

effects.log: You sit on the mound with your face as it comes. It is a very long night. Toward morning it settles. You look at your hands, and they are quite small, and you do not mind them. You go down before anyone is up.

choices.text: Break the bowl. Wash by touch, and see no one you do not know

effects.log: You hold the face on by habit, and by salt, and by being very regular in your ways. It is like carrying a full jar. You can do that. You have been doing that all your life.

events.text: {npc} brings you up at last to the oldest mound of all, at moonrise, and goes to sit some way off. Somebody is already there: a small, plain, elderly person on a stone, easing one knee. They look like your whole lane. They look you over, with the same patience you use, and you feel your mouth go to one side. Then you feel them see that. {bk_anc} reaches over, and pushes your left ear down with one dry thumb.

choices.text: Let your face go, in front of it, and see

effects.log: It slides. You have never done this with another soul watching. It lets its own go too, and there in the moonlight are two foxes, very tired. It breathes out. So you are not the only one.

choices.text: Hold yours on. Bow, as to an old friend of the house

effects.log: You bow very well. It bows back, just as well. You could go on like this until dawn, each as polite and convincing as the other, and you do. {npc} says it was the most frightening thing {he} has ever sat through.

events.text: You wake knowing that you are wanted, up at the old mound. There is no one on the stone this time. There are two things on it, set out rather carefully in the moonlight: a mask in old alder, worn so thin that the moon comes through, with no expression on it that you can name; and half of a dry gourd. That is all that is left. {npc} will not go near. A very long way off, a dog begins to bark.

choices.text: Take the mask, and hold it up to your face

effects.log: It fits. It would fit anyone, you know that, and you hold it there anyway. It smells of someone's thumbs. When you take it down your face has stopped hurting, in a place that you had not known was hurting.

choices.text: Take the half gourd, and drink from it at the first stream

effects.log: Water out of it tastes of old wine, faintly, and then only of water. Something drank from it once, in front of a whole village, with a bead in its mouth. You keep it on the shelf, and you use it.

events.text: You are tired of being liked. {npc} has walked you out to the crossroads, and you have no idea what your face is doing. "You are wearing thin," {he} says. "You could spit out that bead, and be one person, with a nose, until you die. Dogs would come to you. Or you could turn over three times, here, and go up the hill and not come down. A third way wants a lot of keeping up. I have only known it done in a story."

choices.text: Spit it out

effects.log: It goes into the ditch with a very small click. You have a nose, and it is not a good one. That evening you go down the lane, and a dog looks up, and thinks about it.

choices.text: Turn over three times

effects.log: Once for the house, and once for the name, and the third is for nothing at all. Someone finds your good coat in the road, and everyone is sure that it belonged to their cousin.

choices.text: Keep it. Be a fox with a house, and let them know it

effects.log: You go home and tell them. Some of them knew. You keep one face from now on, and you let it slip when you are tired. {npc} says it is a lot of trouble, and that somebody once stood by a lamp for this.

events.text: A dog has come to you. It is a stupid brown dog with one ear, it has started following you up the lane, and now it has put its whole head in your lap. You do not know what to do with your hands. You have a bad nose and a plain voice, and no idea what anyone is thinking. People find you rather ordinary, and they have stopped asking you to weddings. {npc} comes by, stops at the gate, and has to go away again.

choices.text: Scratch the ear. Stay there until your leg goes numb

effects.log: It sighs, and it stays. Your leg goes numb. You are too frightened to move it, and you keep it there most of the afternoon. That dog lives another eleven years.

choices.text: Go to the next wedding anyway, uninvited, as yourself

effects.log: No one knows quite who you are. You say something, and it is wrong, and someone's uncle looks at you with dislike. You go home glowing. Someone has disliked you, personally.

events.text: You sit up on the mounds at the full moon with the bead going round in your mouth. You do not need anything. But there is a festival at the foot of the hill, you can smell the oil, and you are down there in a face before you have decided, as someone's cousin, just for the evening. Everyone is glad to see you. {npc} is on the bench by the gate, and {he} moves over without looking up. A dog leaves.

choices.text: Sit. Have the fried cakes, and ask after everybody

effects.log: You know all their names, and all their troubles. You go home before light with grease on your tail, quite sure that you will not do it again until next year.

choices.text: Go back up before you have sat down

effects.log: You turn at the gate. It is very clear on the mound, and the moon is good. You can still smell the oil from there. A person could get used to that, and you have.

events.text: You keep a house with your tail out. Everyone in the lane knows, and they have agreed not to mention it, except when they want something found. You have one dog, and it hates you. It growls at you every morning from the doorstep, and it has not left in nine years. {npc} thinks that this is the funniest thing in the county.

choices.text: Feed it yourself, and let it growl

effects.log: It takes the food out of your hand, growling. One cold night it comes and lies down against the tails, still growling, and you both go to sleep without mentioning it.

choices.text: Go round the lane and settle what wants settling, in your fur

effects.log: You know who is lying, and you say so, and nobody is under any illusion. It is much less work. They seem to like you about half as much, and that half is real.

events.text: The faces have started to get muddled. Sometimes you are talking to a small one of the house in the voice of a ferryman, dead these sixty years, and you can't tell how long you have been at it. They do not mind. They like the ferryman. Today the smallest asks what you looked like when you were young. {npc} looks up, everyone looks up, you open your mouth, and you find that you do not know.

choices.text: Say so

effects.log: "I do not know," you say. The child thinks that over, goes for a bit of charcoal, and draws you on the step: a round thing with ears. You keep looking at it until the rain takes it. It is very like.

choices.text: Do the ferryman again

effects.log: They laugh so much. You do the comb-seller, and the one who owed money. They beg for more. {npc} looks at you over their heads, and you go on until you are too tired, and nobody knows a thing.

events.text: You are nearly done. They have come to sit with you, from three villages. They each bend down and look, and you hear them at the door. "The image of my grandfather," says one. "The image of my aunt," says another. They are all quite sure. {npc} wipes your mouth, looks at something there, and says nothing. It is very quiet. Out in the yard, a dog has come as far as the door.

choices.text: Let them go on. Everyone should have somebody to look like

effects.log: They go on, quite happily, all that day. You have been so many people's kin. It was the only real work you ever did, and you did it well, and you are not sorry.

choices.text: Call the dog

effects.log: It stands in the door for a long time with its ears forward. You do not call twice. You lie with your hand over the edge of the mat, open, and you wait. You have learned how long to wait.
